section_titles: Calendar and months of the year
periods.activity_title: Building July: Filling a Real Calendar Grid

tasks_in_class.description: Make the calendar for the month of July 2024 by filling the blank grid.
Observe the July month and write the number of Sundays.
Write the dates in July that are Thursdays.

time_bands.activity: Open with the story of a family finding July missing from their calendar. Distribute a blank July 2024 grid and discuss: what do students already know about July — where it falls, how many days? Children identify that July has 31 days and that July 1, 2024 falls on a Monday, then begin filling the grid.

Let us Do, p.166 ("Make the calendar for July 2024 by filling the blank grid.") Children work in pairs, placing each date in the correct column for its day. The teacher circulates, asking: 'How do you know Monday comes first this week?' Children complete the full grid.

Let us Do Q1, p.166 ("Observe the July month and write the number of Sundays.") and Let us Do Q2, p.166 ("Write the dates in July that are Thursdays.") Children scan their completed grid, circle each Sunday, count them, and then list Thursday dates. Pairs compare answers and discuss any disagreements before a quick whole-class check.

periods.teacher_notes: Children commonly confuse the day a month starts with the day they place first in the grid — reinforce that the column must match the day name at the top. The activity of counting Sundays and listing Thursdays consolidates that they can navigate a grid they have built themselves. Linking the family story to a real blank grid gives the calendar immediate meaning.
materials: Printed blank July 2024 calendar grids (one per pair)
A completed reference July 2024 calendar for the teacher

section_titles: Calendar and months of the year
periods.activity_title: Counting Forward: Date Arithmetic on July

tasks_in_class.description: Three days after July 22 is July ___. The day on this date is ___.
A school closes on July 7 for 15 days. Find the date on which the school will open.

time_bands.activity: Children display their July 2024 grids or use a shared class display of the completed July calendar. The teacher poses a warm-up: 'Point to July 10. What day is it? What about two days later?' Children count forward on the grid, establishing the counting-on method.

Let us Do Q3, p.166 ("Three days after July 22 is July ___. The day on this date is ___.") Children place a finger on July 22 and count three steps forward on the grid. They write the date and name the day. Pairs discuss: did they count July 22 itself, or start from the next day? The teacher clarifies the 'three days after' convention.

Let us Do Q4, p.166 ("A school closes on July 7 for 15 days. Find the date on which the school will open.") Children locate July 7 and count forward 15 days on their grids, recording each count. The teacher asks: 'After July 31, where do we go?' guiding those who notice the month ends. A whole-class share confirms the answer and the counting method used.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is counting July 7 itself as day one, arriving at an answer one day early — ask children to point at each counted date aloud. The problem that crosses the month boundary (15 days from July 7) naturally raises the question of what comes after July, previewing the work on months ahead. Children who finish early can pose their own 'how many days after' questions using the grid.
materials: Completed July 2024 calendar grids from the previous unit or a fresh printed copy

periods.activity_title: Same or Different? Comparing Two Year Calendars

tasks_in_class.description: Collect calendars for last two years. Observe what is the same and what changes; tick (a) Names of months (b) Days in a month (c) Days in a week (d) Number of Sundays (e) Number of weeks.
Fill in festival dates (Deepawali, Ganesh Chaturthi, etc.) for two years in DD/MM/YY format and circle the festivals that fall on the same date.

time_bands.activity: Distribute one calendar for each of two different years to each group of four. The teacher asks: 'Without looking closely — do you think these calendars are the same or different?' Groups share predictions. The teacher lists predicted 'same' and 'different' items on the board.

Let us Explore, p.167 ("Collect calendars for last two years. Observe what is the same and what changes; tick (a)–(e).") Groups open both calendars to January and compare each item in the list. They tick whether it stays the same or changes, justifying each tick: 'The names of months are the same in both — January, February…'. The teacher prompts: 'What about the number of Sundays in January?'

Let us Explore, p.167 ("Fill in festival dates for two years in DD/MM/YY format and circle festivals that fall on the same date.") Each group lists three or four festivals they know, looks up the date in each calendar, records it in DD/MM/YY format, and circles any that share the same date across years. A brief share: 'Which festivals moved? Which stayed fixed?'

periods.teacher_notes: Children often assume all festivals repeat on the same date each year — the exercise of recording actual dates across two calendars builds evidence for the fixed versus movable distinction. Encourage groups to justify why names of months do not change ('the calendar's structure stays the same') versus why the number of Sundays can differ ('it depends where the month starts'). Having two physical calendars side by side is essential for this comparison.
materials: One printed or real calendar for each of two different years per group (groups of 4)
Chalkboard or whiteboard for class list

periods.activity_title: Months, Days, and Weeks: The Year's Structure

tasks_in_class.description: Write the names of the 12 months in a year.
Write the months that have less than 30 days.
Write the number of days in a year.
Hetal says there are 53 weeks in a year. Is she right? Yes/No. If not, how many weeks are in a year?

time_bands.activity: Children write the 12 months in order from memory: Let us Do Q1, p.167 ("Write the names of the 12 months in a year.") The teacher invites volunteers to recite the sequence and writes each month on the board as it is named. Groups check their own lists against the board.

Let us Do Q2, p.167 ("Write the months that have less than 30 days.") and Let us Do Q3, p.167 ("Write the number of days in a year.") Children use the calendars available to count the days in each month, then identify months with fewer than 30. They add all 12 months' days to find the year total, recording their addition.

Let us Do Q4, p.167 ("Hetal says there are 53 weeks in a year. Is she right?") Children divide 365 by 7 informally — using repeated subtraction or a chart — to find how many complete weeks fit into 365 days and how many days remain. They discuss: 'Is Hetal right? How do you know?' Groups share their reasoning; the class reaches a consensus on the number of weeks and the extra days.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is claiming February has fewer than 30 days and stopping there — prompt children to check every month, including ones that might seem obviously 30 or 31. When children work out 365 ÷ 7, expect a range of informal strategies; accept repeated subtraction, grouping sevens, or using a calendar row count, and discuss why they all arrive at the same answer. The Hetal puzzle is well suited to pair discussion before whole-class resolution.
materials: Calendars for reference (same as unit 3 or fresh copies)
Squared or plain paper for addition working

section_titles: Age and dates using birth certificates
periods.activity_title: Reading Bincy's Birth Certificate: Dates and Age

tasks_in_class.description: Talk to your mother and find: my age, my mother's age today, her age when I was born, my mother's mother's age today, when my mother was born, and when I was born.
2/5/2015 shows that Bincy was born on 2 (April/May/June/July) in the year 2015.
How old will Bincy be on 2 May 2025?

homework.description: Talk to your mother and find: my age, my mother's age today, her age when I was born, my mother's mother's age today, when my mother was born, and when I was born.

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the idea of a birth certificate and the DD/MM/YY date format. Children discuss: 'What information does a birth certificate carry? What does 02/05/2015 mean?' The class works out together which number is the day, which the month, and which the year.

Let us Do Q1, p.169 ("2/5/2015 shows that Bincy was born on 2 (April/May/June/July) in the year 2015.") Children examine Bincy's birth certificate in the textbook and identify which month number 5 names. They discuss why the format can be confusing if day and month are mixed up, and confirm that 5 = May.

Let us Do Q2, p.169 ("How old will Bincy be on 2 May 2025?") Children calculate Bincy's age by subtracting her birth year from 2025, then confirm that the date 2 May has arrived (it is her birthday). The teacher asks: 'What operation are we using?' Children write their working. The Age Fun activity, p.168, is introduced as a home interview to carry out with their mother.

periods.teacher_notes: Children frequently confuse the day and month fields in DD/MM/YY format — emphasise that the position matters, not just the number. The subtraction for age is straightforward but children should state the full reasoning ('Born 2015, turning 10 in 2025, because 2025 − 2015 = 10'). The Age Fun interview is set as homework so children bring back real data for the next work on three-generation ages.

section_titles: Age and dates using birth certificates

tasks_in_class.description: How old will she be in 2030?
Eighth birthday of Bincy was on ___.
Bincy was ___ months old on 2 August 2015.
Hetal is twice as old as her brother and also 10 years older. Guess the age of Hetal and her brother.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q3, p.169 ("How old will she be in 2030?") and Let us Do Q4, p.169 ("Eighth birthday of Bincy was on ___.") Children continue working with Bincy's birth date. For Q3 they subtract 2015 from 2030. For Q4 they add 8 years to her birth year and keep the same date: 2 May. The teacher asks 'Why does the day and month stay the same for a birthday?'

Let us Do Q5, p.169 ("Bincy was ___ months old on 2 August 2015.") Children count: Bincy was born on 2 May 2015; 2 August 2015 is the next occurrence. They count month by month — May to June, June to July, July to August — arriving at 3 months. The teacher emphasises that the day of the month is the same (the 2nd), so each step is exactly one month.

Age Fun, p.168 ("Hetal is twice as old as her brother and also 10 years older. Guess the age of Hetal and her brother.") Children work in pairs, trying different ages for the brother and checking both conditions. The teacher encourages a systematic guess-and-check approach: 'If the brother is 5, is Hetal twice that? Is she also 10 more?' Pairs share their answers and reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: Children may struggle with the two-condition age puzzle — guide them to set up a small table of guesses rather than trying to solve it in one step. The months-old calculation is a new type of counting (months rather than years), so make the counting-on explicit: 'May is month 0, June is month 1…'. Connecting this months-counting to the 12-months sequence reinforces calendar structure built earlier in the chapter.

section_titles: Age and dates using birth certificates
periods.activity_title: My Own Birth Certificate and School Dates

tasks_in_class.description: After how many days of her birth was the certificate issued?
Make your own birth certificate filling in name, sex, date of birth, place, parents' names, date of making certificate, and age on that date.
Complete the table by writing: date of birth, date admitted to school, date admitted to Class 1, date admitted to Class 3.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q6, p.169 ("After how many days of her birth was the certificate issued?") Using Bincy's birth date (2 May 2015) and the certificate issue date (18 May 2015), children count the days between the two dates on a May calendar strip or by counting forward. The teacher models: 'May 2 to May 18 — let us count the days in between.'

Let us Do Q1, p.170 ("Make your own birth certificate filling in name, sex, date of birth, place, parents' names, date of making certificate, and age on that date.") Children fill in the certificate template in the textbook with their own details. The teacher circulates, checking that dates are written in DD/MM/YY format and that age is calculated correctly as the difference between today's year and birth year.

Let us Do Q2, p.170 ("Complete the table by writing: date of birth, date admitted to school, date admitted to Class 1, date admitted to Class 3.") Children recall or estimate these key dates from their own school history and record them in DD/MM/YY format. If children are unsure, the teacher suggests they can leave a field with a question mark and ask a family member later.

periods.teacher_notes: The days-between calculation is the first time children count days within a single month between two given dates — emphasise that they count the days strictly between the two dates, not including the start date itself, or use the 'bigger minus smaller' approach and discuss whether it gives the same answer. Children who cannot recall their admission dates should not be distressed; the personal certificate activity is about applying the DD/MM/YY format to real data, and an approximate year is sufficient. Having a simple May calendar strip on the board supports the counting task.
materials: A printed May 2015 calendar strip or small calendar on the board

periods.activity_title: Watching the Hands: Exploring an Analog Clock

tasks_in_class.description: Get a working analog clock or watch. Observe the face and movements of the hands; discuss what you observe.
Hetal started breakfast at 07:00 and finished at 07:15. She took ___ minutes; how do you know?

time_bands.activity: Let us Play, p.171 ("Get a working analog clock or watch. Observe the face and movements of the hands; discuss what you observe.") Groups of four receive an analog clock. The teacher asks: 'How many hands? Which moves faster? What do the numbers mean?' Children observe for a short period, then share: one group reports on the hands, another on the numbers, a third on the movement direction.

The teacher sets the clock to 12:00 and moves the minute hand, asking children to track its position at each 5-minute mark. Children identify which numbers the minute hand points to at 5, 10, 15 minutes past. The vocabulary 'quarter past' and 'half past' is introduced by the teacher: 'When the minute hand reaches 3, that is quarter past the hour.'

Let us Do Q1, p.171 ("Hetal started breakfast at 07:00 and finished at 07:15. She took ___ minutes; how do you know?") Children look at two clock face images in the textbook showing 07:00 and 07:15, count the minute-hand movement from 12 to 3 (5+5+5 = 15), and write their answer with a brief explanation. Pairs share their 'how do you know' reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often confuse the hour hand and minute hand at first — the longer hand is the minute hand, and connecting its length to 'more detail' (minutes are smaller divisions than hours) is a helpful anchor. The 'how do you know?' prompt for the breakfast-duration task is important: accept counting by fives, counting individual marks, or reading the numbers directly, and discuss why all three routes agree. A clock with a visible, movable minute hand is essential for this unit.
materials: One working analog clock or demonstration clock per group of 4

periods.activity_title: Drawing Hands: Quarter Past, Half Past, and Daily Time

tasks_in_class.description: Draw the hour hand and minute hand on the clock to show 8:15 or quarter past 8.
Draw the hour hand and minute hand on the clock to show 8:30 or half past 8.
A Day in the life of Hetal: match each activity to its time, write the missing o'clock times, and draw hands on blank clock faces.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q2(a), p.171 ("Draw the hour hand and minute hand on the clock to show 8:15 or quarter past 8.") The teacher first sets the demonstration clock to 8:15, asking children to name where each hand points. Children then draw both hands on the blank clock face in the textbook. The teacher checks that the hour hand is drawn slightly past 8, not exactly on it.

Let us Do Q2(b), p.171 ("Draw the hour hand and minute hand on the clock to show 8:30 or half past 8.") The same process — teacher sets the demonstration clock, children observe, then draw. The teacher highlights that the hour hand is now halfway between 8 and 9. Children compare their 8:15 and 8:30 drawings: 'What moved? What moved more?'

Let us Do, p.172 ("A Day in the life of Hetal: match each activity to its time, write the missing o'clock times, and draw hands on blank clock faces.") Children work individually through all eight daily activities — matching, writing times, and drawing hands. The teacher circulates and addresses any confusion about o'clock positions. A brief whole-class review of one or two completed clock faces closes the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Children frequently place the hour hand exactly on the hour numeral even when the time is quarter or half past — emphasise that the hour hand moves continuously and sits between two numbers at quarter and half past. The 'Day in the life of Hetal' integrates reading and drawing, so children encounter both directions of the skill in one activity; allow children to use the demonstration clock as a reference tool while drawing. Having the demonstration clock visible throughout this unit is important.
materials: Pencils and rulers for drawing clock hands

section_titles: Duration of time — minutes, hours, days, months
periods.activity_title: How Long Does It Take? Classifying Duration

tasks_in_class.description: Fill the table with events from daily life under: takes months, takes weeks, takes days, takes hours, takes minutes.
Write the number of minutes taken for: school period, lunch break, mid-day meal, play period, eating dinner, brushing teeth.

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the 'Visit to Nani's House' comic strip from page 173 with the class, pausing at each duration mentioned ('Nani knitted my sweater for months', 'The vegetables were grown in weeks'). The class discusses: 'Why months for a sweater? Why not hours?' establishing that different events require different duration units.

Let us Think, p.173 ("Fill the table with events from daily life under: takes months, takes weeks, takes days, takes hours, takes minutes.") In small groups children brainstorm events and place each in a column. The teacher circulates with prompting questions: 'Growing a plant — hours or weeks? A maths lesson — days or minutes?' Groups share one or two entries per column.

Let us Do Q3, p.174 ("Write the number of minutes taken for: school period, lunch break, mid-day meal, play period, eating dinner, brushing teeth.") Children draw on their own experience to estimate and record each duration in minutes. The teacher asks: 'How did you decide? Did you count, estimate, or know it?' Brief class discussion compares different children's estimates for the same activity.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often place activities in the wrong column because they confuse the duration of one instance with an ongoing process — 'eating breakfast' takes minutes, but 'getting ready for school' might feel like longer; prompt them to think about a single occasion. For the minutes task, there is no single correct answer for activities like 'eating dinner' — the aim is reasoned estimation, and disagreements between children are productive. The comic strip is a bridge from the familiar to the mathematical.
materials: Chalkboard for a shared class version of the duration table

section_titles: Duration of time — minutes, hours, days, months
periods.activity_title: What Fits in Five Minutes? Elapsed Time on Clock Faces

tasks_in_class.description: Write down what you can do in each time frame: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 45, 60 minutes.
Write the number of minutes passed by looking at the movement of minute and hour hands across 6 pairs of start-and-end clock faces.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q4, p.174 ("Write down what you can do in each time frame: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 45, 60 minutes.") Pairs brainstorm and record one activity per time frame. The teacher then asks a few pairs to share: 'What did you put for 5 minutes? For 60?' The class checks whether the suggestions feel reasonable — 'Could you really cook a meal in 5 minutes?'

Let us Do Q5, p.175 ("Write the number of minutes passed by looking at the movement of minute and hour hands across 6 pairs of start-and-end clock faces.") Children work through each pair of clock faces — reading the start time, reading the end time, and counting the minute-hand movement to find elapsed minutes. The teacher demonstrates the first pair: 'The minute hand moved from 12 to 3 — that is 15 minutes.' Children complete the remaining five pairs independently, then compare answers with a partner.

periods.teacher_notes: Children may subtract clock numerals directly (e.g. '9 − 6 = 3 minutes') rather than multiplying by 5 — the key correction is that each number on the clock face represents 5 minutes, not 1. The time-frame brainstorm is open and personal, so all reasonable answers should be accepted; the purpose is to connect lived experience to a numerical quantity. Linking this elapsed-time reading to the earlier breakfast-duration work (on clock faces showing 07:00 and 07:15) gives the clock-face method a familiar anchor.

section_titles: Digital and analog clocks; making a sand clock
periods.activity_title: Digital vs Analog: Two Clocks, One Time

tasks_in_class.description: What is the difference between the digital clock and the analog clock shown?
Which clock do you have on your school wall?

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws or displays images of a digital clock (e.g. showing 18:02) and an analog clock on the board. Children observe both: 'What do you notice? What is different about the way they show the time?' Children pair-share their observations before a whole-class listing on the board.

Let us Explore Q1, p.176 ("What is the difference between the digital clock and the analog clock shown?") Children write their answer in their own words, drawing on the textbook images. The teacher prompts: 'How does the digital clock show 6 minutes past 6 in the evening differently from the analog?' and introduces the idea of digits versus hands.

Let us Explore Q2, p.176 ("Which clock do you have on your school wall?") Children discuss and agree on the type of clock in their classroom. The teacher then extends: 'Have you seen a digital clock at home? A railway station? A microwave?' The class connects clock type to context, discussing where each is more convenient. Children record their answer to Q2 and note one context for each clock type.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have only seen digital clocks may struggle to articulate the analog clock's advantage for reading elapsed time visually — use the demonstration analog clock to show the minute hand sweeping through an arc, pointing out that you can see 'how much time has gone'. The 18:02 format on a digital clock is a natural opening to discuss 24-hour time informally ('18 means 6 in the evening') without requiring formal conversion. The school-wall clock question grounds the abstract comparison in immediate experience.
materials: Images of a digital clock (showing e.g. 18:02) and an analog clock on the board or textbook p.176

section_titles: Digital and analog clocks; making a sand clock
periods.activity_title: Build a Sand Clock: Measuring Duration by Hand

tasks_in_class.description: Make your own sand clock using two transparent bottles with joined caps and fine sand; find out how long the sand takes to shift by looking at the clock.

time_bands.activity: The teacher presents the two joined-bottle sand clock from the textbook (p.176) and asks: 'How is this like a clock? What does the sand measure? How is it different from the analog clock we used?' The class discusses non-standard versus standard timers, linking to the idea that any regular process can measure duration.

Let us Explore, p.176 ("Make your own sand clock using two transparent bottles with joined caps and fine sand; find out how long the sand takes to shift by looking at the clock.") Groups assemble their sand clocks using the pre-glued bottle caps with a small hole provided. They fill the top bottle with a measured portion of fine sand, then flip and time the transfer against an analog clock, recording the time it takes.

Groups share their results: 'Our sand clock took ___ minutes.' The class compares: do all sand clocks take the same time? Children discuss what might cause differences (amount of sand, size of hole). The teacher closes by asking: 'Could you use your sand clock to time a game? What would you need to know?' connecting back to the duration-classification work done in the sections on minutes, hours, days, and months.

periods.teacher_notes: Pre-glue the bottle caps with a small, consistent hole before the unit to ensure the sand flows at a measurable rate — variability in hole size is the main source of differences between groups, and this is a productive comparison rather than a problem. Children may not know how to time an event against a clock if they have not done so before; demonstrate the start-and-stop reading explicitly. The sand clock brings together the concrete measurement of duration that runs through the entire chapter, from calendar counting to elapsed clock-face minutes.
materials: Two transparent plastic bottles per group with caps glued together and a small hole drilled
Demonstration analog clock or wall clock

periods.activity_title: Time All Around: A Chapter-Wide Time Challenge

time_bands.activity: The teacher places four large labels on the board: CALENDAR, AGE AND DATES, CLOCK, DURATION. Each label names a strand from the chapter. Children pair-share one thing they remember about each strand, then the class contributes one idea per strand to build a quick four-column summary on the board. This activates the full span of the chapter before the challenge begins.

Groups of four receive a 'Time Challenge' card with four linked problems, one per strand: (a) A month-grid question — 'A school trip is on the 3rd Sunday of August 2024. August 1 is a Thursday. What is the date of the trip?' (b) An age question — 'Ravi was born on 10 March 2014. How old will he be on 10 March 2026?' (c) A clock question — 'Draw hands on a blank clock face to show 4:45.' (d) A duration question — 'Priya practises music for 35 minutes each day. She starts at 5:00 pm. At what time does she finish?' Each group works through all four, recording their method alongside each answer.

Each group shares one answer with the class, explaining their method: 'We used the calendar grid to count Sundays'; 'We subtracted birth year from target year'; 'We put the minute hand at 9 for 45 minutes past'; 'We counted forward 35 minutes from 5:00'. The teacher connects each method to the tools of the chapter — calendar, birth certificate, analog clock, elapsed time — and closes by returning to the dissolution question: 'Which tool did each problem need? Why?'

periods.teacher_notes: The four-problem challenge is designed so that each group member can lead on one strand — assign ownership before they begin so every child contributes. Accept varied methods: the calendar grid can be sketched from memory or counted on fingers for the August problem; the clock-drawing can use a blank circle drawn freehand. The goal is to surface the connections between the chapter's tools and contexts, not to produce uniform working.
materials: Printed 'Time Challenge' cards (one per group of 4)
Blank clock face circles (printed or drawn on the card)

items.section_title: Calendar and months of the year
items.prompt: Look at the blank calendar grid below. August 1, 2024 is a Thursday. Fill in the dates for the first two weeks of August 2024 (1st to 14th) in the correct boxes.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 1: Sun blank, Mon blank, Tue blank, Wed blank, Thu 1, Fri 2, Sat 3. Row 2: Sun 4, Mon 5, Tue 6, Wed 7, Thu 8, Fri 9, Sat 10. Row 3 first four: Sun 11, Mon 12, Tue 13, Wed 14.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place 1 in the Thursday column and fill each subsequent date in the next cell, wrapping to the next row after Saturday.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may use a number line 1–14 and point at each; stretch: add dates 15–31 and name the day of August 31.

exercise.description: Make the calendar for the month of July 2024 by filling the blank grid.

items.section_title: Comparing calendars across years
items.prompt: Arjun looks at two calendars — one for 2023 and one for 2024. He says: 'One thing is definitely the same in both calendars.' Which of the following is always the same in any two calendars for different years?

options.label: A
options.text: The number of Sundays in January

options.label: C
options.text: The date on which Diwali falls

options.label: D
options.text: The day on which January 1 falls

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The names of the 12 months (Option B).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare what is fixed by the calendar's structure versus what depends on the year's starting day.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not yet understood that the number of Sundays depends on which day a month starts, which changes across years.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has not yet grasped that some festivals are movable and change date across years.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may believe the calendar repeats identically each year, not realising that January 1 falls on a different day each year.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can open two real calendars and check each option one by one; stretch: find one more thing that always stays the same and one more that always changes.

exercise.description: Collect calendars for last two years. Observe what is the same and what changes; tick (a) Names of months (b) Days in a month (c) Days in a week (d) Number of Sundays (e) Number of weeks.

items.section_title: Age and dates using birth certificates
items.prompt: Meena's birth certificate shows her date of birth as 14/03/2016. Write what each number in her date of birth means. Then write her date of birth in words.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 14 is the day; 03 is the month (March); 2016 is the year. Meena was born on the fourteenth of March, 2016.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: In DD/MM/YY format, the first number is the day, the middle number is the month, and the last is the year.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may use a reference list of month numbers 1–12 to identify March = 03; stretch: write their own date of birth in DD/MM/YY format and in words.

exercise.description: Make your own birth certificate filling in name, sex, date of birth, place, parents' names, date of making certificate, and age on that date.

items.section_title: Reading clock time — analog clocks
items.prompt: Look at an analog clock face. Where is the minute hand pointing when the time is exactly 3 o'clock? Where is the hour hand pointing? Write one thing you notice about the two hands at o'clock times.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: At 3 o'clock: the minute hand points straight up to 12, and the hour hand points to 3. At every o'clock time the minute hand is always at 12.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: At any o'clock time the minute hand completes a full round and returns to 12, while the hour hand moves to the next number.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may use a real or demonstration clock set to 3:00 to observe the hands directly; stretch: describe where the hands are at 6 o'clock and 9 o'clock and state the pattern.

exercise.description: Get a working analog clock or watch. Observe the face and movements of the hands; discuss what you observe.

items.section_title: Digital and analog clocks; making a sand clock
items.prompt: Riya made a sand clock at home. She found that the sand shifted from the top bottle to the bottom bottle in 2 minutes. She wants to time a 6-minute activity. What should she do with her sand clock? Explain your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: She should flip the sand clock 3 times, because each flip measures 2 minutes, and 3 flips give 3 × 2 = 6 minutes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the number of flips by the time per flip to reach the total duration needed.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can act it out by counting: flip once = 2 min, flip again = 4 min, flip again = 6 min; stretch: how many flips for 10 minutes? Is it possible exactly?

exercise.description: Make your own sand clock using two transparent bottles with joined caps and fine sand; find out how long the sand takes to shift by looking at the clock.

items.section_title: Calendar and months of the year
items.prompt: In a particular month, the first day is a Wednesday. How many Wednesdays are there in that month if it has 31 days? Show your working using the calendar grid idea.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The Wednesdays fall on dates 1, 8, 15, 22, 29 — that is 5 Wednesdays.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Starting from date 1 on Wednesday, add 7 each time to find all Wednesdays within 31 days.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can sketch a simple 7-column grid and fill in dates starting from Wednesday; stretch: if the month had 30 days instead, would the number of Wednesdays change?

exercise.description: Write the dates in July that are Thursdays.

items.section_title: Comparing calendars across years
items.prompt: Independence Day (15 August) is a fixed-date festival. Eid-ul-Fitr falls on a different date each year. Which of the following correctly explains the difference?

options.label: A
options.text: Independence Day falls on 15 August every year because it follows the solar calendar; Eid-ul-Fitr follows a different calendar so its date changes each year.

options.label: B
options.text: Both festivals follow the same calendar so both change their date each year.

options.label: C
options.text: Independence Day changes its date every year just like Eid-ul-Fitr.

options.label: D
options.text: Eid-ul-Fitr falls on the same date every year because it is an important festival.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option A — Independence Day is fixed on 15 August every year; Eid-ul-Fitr follows a different calendar and its date shifts each year.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the two years' entries for each festival: same date each year means fixed; different dates mean movable.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has not yet grasped that some festivals are fixed to a date while others are tied to a different calendar system.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student incorrectly believes national holidays can shift date, perhaps confusing observed-holiday adjustments with the festival date itself.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is reasoning from the festival's importance rather than from its calendar basis, a common intuitive error at this stage.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can check two calendars for 15 August in both years to confirm it stays the same; stretch: name one more fixed-date and one more movable festival from their own experience and explain how they know.

exercise.description: Fill in festival dates (Deepawali, Ganesh Chaturthi, etc.) for two years in DD/MM/YY format and circle the festivals that fall on the same date.

items.section_title: Comparing calendars across years
items.prompt: A year has 365 days. Pooja says there are 52 complete weeks and 1 extra day in a year. Is she correct?

options.label: B
options.text: No, because 53 × 7 = 371 which is more than 365.

options.label: C
options.text: No, because a year has exactly 53 weeks with no extra days.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option A — 52 × 7 = 364, so there is 1 day remaining, meaning 52 complete weeks and 1 extra day.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply 52 by 7 to get 364, then subtract from 365 to find the remainder.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student correctly identifies that 53 full weeks overshoot 365 but draws the wrong conclusion about Pooja's statement, not recognising the 52 + 1 structure.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused 52 complete weeks plus an extra day with the claim of 53 full weeks, perhaps from earlier discussion of the topic.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has made an arithmetic error, believing 52 × 7 = 365 instead of 364.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can group 365 into bundles of 7 using repeated subtraction; stretch: in a leap year with 366 days, how many complete weeks and how many extra days are there?

exercise.description: Hetal says there are 53 weeks in a year. Is she right? Yes/No. If not, how many weeks are in a year?

items.section_title: Age and dates using birth certificates
items.prompt: A birth certificate shows a date written as 07/11/2018. Which of the following correctly reads this date?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option A — in DD/MM/YY format, 07 is the day, 11 is the month (November), and 2018 is the year.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: In DD/MM/YY, the first pair is the day, the second pair is the month number, and the last four digits are the year.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has swapped day and month, reading MM/DD instead of DD/MM — a very common confusion with international date formats.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has merged parts of the date incorrectly, treating the year as split across positions.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has misread 11 as February (perhaps associating 11 with the 2nd month somehow) or has confused month numbering.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may use a month-number reference chart (1 = January … 12 = December); stretch: write three different dates in DD/MM/YY format and read each aloud to a partner.

exercise.description: 2/5/2015 shows that Bincy was born on 2 (April/May/June/July) in the year 2015.

items.section_title: Age and dates using birth certificates
items.prompt: Kavya is twice as old as her sister and also 6 years older than her sister. How old is each of them? Show your guesses and checking.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Sister is 6 years old; Kavya is 12 years old. Check: 12 = 2 × 6 (twice the sister's age) and 12 − 6 = 6 (6 years older).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Try ages for the sister; Kavya must be exactly twice that age AND exactly 6 more — keep guessing until both conditions are met.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can use a guess-and-check table with columns: sister's age, twice sister's age, difference; stretch: what if Kavya were 3 times as old and 8 years older — find the ages.

exercise.description: Hetal is twice as old as her brother and also 10 years older. Guess the age of Hetal and her brother.

items.section_title: Reading clock time — analog clocks
items.prompt: Mohan looked at a clock and saw the minute hand pointing to 6 and the hour hand pointing between 2 and 3. What time is it? How do you know what the minute hand at 6 means?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The time is 2:30 (half past 2). The minute hand at 6 means 30 minutes past the hour, because from 12 to 6 is half the clock face, which is 6 × 5 = 30 minutes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each number on the clock face represents 5 minutes; the minute hand at 6 is 6 × 5 = 30 minutes past the hour.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can use a demonstration clock and count the 5-minute marks from 12 to 6 aloud; stretch: what time would it be if the hour hand were between 7 and 8 and the minute hand at 6?

exercise.description: Hetal started breakfast at 07:00 and finished at 07:15. She took ___ minutes; how do you know?

items.section_title: Duration of time — minutes, hours, days, months
items.prompt: Which of the following activities would most likely take hours rather than minutes or days?

options.label: B
options.text: A road journey from one city to another

options.label: C
options.text: Growing a plant from a seed

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option B — a road journey from one city to another typically takes several hours.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the activity to the appropriate unit by thinking about how long the activity actually lasts in real life.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may not yet have internalised that teeth-brushing is a very short activity measured in minutes, not hours.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused 'hours' with longer durations; growing a plant takes weeks or months, not hours.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be guessing rather than reasoning about duration; blinking takes less than a second, far shorter than a minute.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can use the five-column table (months/weeks/days/hours/minutes) as a reference and place each option into a column first; stretch: give one example each of an activity taking about 2 hours and about 2 days, and explain how you know.

exercise.description: Fill the table with events from daily life under: takes months, takes weeks, takes days, takes hours, takes minutes.

items.section_title: Digital and analog clocks; making a sand clock
items.prompt: A digital clock shows 14:30. An analog clock in the same room shows the same time. Describe what each clock looks like at this moment. What is the same and what is different about how they show 14:30?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The digital clock displays the digits 14:30. The analog clock has the minute hand pointing to 6 (30 minutes) and the hour hand pointing between 2 and 3 (since 14:30 is 2:30 in the afternoon). Both show the same moment in time. The digital clock uses digits; the analog clock uses the position of two hands.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert 14:30 to 2:30 pm for the analog clock (14 − 12 = 2), then place the hands accordingly.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may use a demonstration analog clock set to 2:30 and describe it; stretch: show what 09:45 would look like on both types of clock.

exercise.description: What is the difference between the digital clock and the analog clock shown?

items.section_title: Reading clock time — analog clocks
items.prompt: Draw the hour hand and minute hand on the blank clock face below to show 3:15 (quarter past 3).

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The minute hand points to 3 (at the 15-minute mark). The hour hand points slightly past 3, between 3 and 4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Quarter past means 15 minutes, so the minute hand goes to 3; the hour hand has moved one quarter of the way from 3 towards 4.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may first set a real clock to 3:15 and copy what they see; stretch: draw the clock for 3:45 and explain where each hand points.

exercise.description: Draw the hour hand and minute hand on the clock to show 8:15 or quarter past 8.

items.section_title: Reading clock time — analog clocks
items.prompt: A clock shows the time for 'school assembly'. The minute hand points to 12 and the hour hand points to 8. Which activity from a school day best matches this time?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option B — 8 o'clock in the morning is a typical time for school assembly.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the hour hand position (8) and the minute hand at 12 (o'clock) to get 8:00, then match to a morning school activity.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has matched the hour 8 to 8 pm or midnight rather than 8 am, not yet connecting clock times to the school day context.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has associated the time with lunch without relating 8 o'clock to morning, possibly guessing from school activities listed.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has not connected 8:00 to a morning context, placing it in the evening without using the activity context as a clue.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can use their 'Day in the life of Hetal' page as a reference for school activity times; stretch: write the clock time for one more school activity and draw the hands on a blank face.

exercise.description: A Day in the life of Hetal: match each activity to its time, write the missing o'clock times, and draw hands on blank clock faces.

items.section_title: Duration of time — minutes, hours, days, months
items.prompt: Which of the following is the most reasonable time for brushing your teeth?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option A — brushing teeth takes about 2 minutes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the activity to the appropriate unit by recalling actual experience of how long the activity lasts.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has not yet connected the unit 'hours' to its actual magnitude relative to a brief daily routine.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be confusing days with a much shorter unit, indicating the duration units have not yet been internalised.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has selected a very large unit for a brief activity, suggesting the scale of weeks versus minutes has not yet been grasped.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can mime brushing teeth while a partner counts slowly to 120 (2 minutes); stretch: estimate the time for three more daily activities and write the unit alongside each.

exercise.description: Write the number of minutes taken for: school period, lunch break, mid-day meal, play period, eating dinner, brushing teeth.

items.section_title: Calendar and months of the year
items.prompt: A school closes on August 20 for 10 days. On which date does the school reopen? (August has 31 days.)

teacher_guide.expected_answer: August 30.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count 10 days forward from August 20: 20 + 10 = 30, so the school reopens on August 30.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can count forward on a drawn August calendar strip one day at a time; stretch: what if the school closed on August 25 for 10 days — which month does it reopen in and on what date?

exercise.description: A school closes on July 7 for 15 days. Find the date on which the school will open.

items.section_title: Comparing calendars across years
items.prompt: How many days are there in a non-leap year? Show how you worked it out using the months.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 365 days. Add: Jan 31 + Feb 28 + Mar 31 + Apr 30 + May 31 + Jun 30 + Jul 31 + Aug 31 + Sep 30 + Oct 31 + Nov 30 + Dec 31 = 365.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the number of days in each of the 12 months (using 28 for February in a non-leap year) to reach 365.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may use a month list with the number of days written beside each month and add in two steps (first half and second half); stretch: what is the total for a leap year and which month changes?

exercise.description: Write the number of days in a year.

items.section_title: Age and dates using birth certificates
items.prompt: Arjun was born on 5 June 2013. How old will he be on 5 June 2027?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the birth year from the target year: 2027 − 2013 = 14.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may count forward from 2013 to 2027 on a number line in yearly steps; stretch: in which year will Arjun turn 18, and on what date will that birthday fall?

exercise.description: How old will Bincy be on 2 May 2025?

items.section_title: Age and dates using birth certificates
items.prompt: Sana was born on 10 April 2020. How many months old was she on 10 July 2020?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 months old. From 10 April to 10 July: April to May = 1 month, May to June = 2 months, June to July = 3 months.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the months from the birth month to the target month, keeping the day of the month the same.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can use a month-name list and point to each step from April to July; stretch: how many months old was Sana on 10 December 2020?

exercise.description: Bincy was ___ months old on 2 August 2015.

items.section_title: Duration of time — minutes, hours, days, months
items.prompt: Look at the two clock faces below. The first shows when Rajan started reading. The second shows when he stopped. How many minutes did he read?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 25 minutes. The minute hand moved from 12 (0 minutes) to 5 (25 minutes): 5 × 5 = 25.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the number of 5-minute steps the minute hand moved from the start position to the end position.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may count individual minute marks from 12 to the 5 on the clock; stretch: if Rajan read for the same amount of time again, what time would the second clock show?

exercise.description: Write the number of minutes passed by looking at the movement of minute and hour hands across 6 pairs of start-and-end clock faces.
